entry:
Branch of physics describing the effect of forces on the motion of macroscopic objects and bulk matter, without considering quantum effects and often without relativistic effects.

It is used to describe projectiles, parts of machinery, spacecraft, planets, stars, galaxies, deformable solids, fluids, and macromolecules. The qualifier *classical* distinguishes it from methods developed after the revolutions in physics of the early 20th century, which revealed its limitations. Some modern sources include relativistic mechanics within it.

The earliest formulation, often called Newtonian mechanics, rests on the 17th-century work of [[Isaac Newton]], whose three laws of motion and law of universal gravitation appeared in 1687, and on mathematical methods developed by Newton, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, [[Leonhard Euler|Euler]], and others. Methods based on energy were developed in the 18th and 19th centuries by Euler, Joseph-Louis Lagrange, William Rowan Hamilton, and others, producing analytical mechanics, which includes [[Lagrangian mechanics]] and [[Hamiltonian mechanics]]. Lagrangian mechanics uses generalized coordinates and velocities; Hamiltonian mechanics uses coordinates and momenta in phase space. The two are equivalent by a Legendre transformation. All equations of motion can be derived from the principle of least action, one consequence of which is [[Noether's theorem]], connecting conservation laws to symmetries.

Traditionally the subject is divided into statics (force and torque on systems in equilibrium), kinematics (the "geometry of motion"), and dynamics, which also considers the forces involved. It can alternatively be divided by region of application: celestial mechanics, continuum mechanics, relativistic mechanics, and statistical mechanics.

If the present state of an object obeying its laws is known, its future and past motion can be determined, although [[Chaos theory]] shows that long-term predictions are unreliable. The theory is accurate for objects that are not extremely massive and whose speeds are far below that of light. Objects about the size of an atom's diameter require [[Quantum mechanics]], speeds approaching that of light require [[Special relativity]], and extremely massive objects require general relativity.

Tradition of art music of the Western world, distinct from Western folk and popular music.

It is characterized by formality and complexity of musical form and harmonic organization, notably the use of polyphony. Since at least the ninth century it has been chiefly a written tradition, with a sophisticated notational system and an accompanying literature of analytical, critical, historical, and philosophical writing. The term is sometimes qualified as *Western classical music* because it can also be applied to non-Western art musics. The English *classical* derives from the Latin *classicus*, originally referring to the highest class of Roman citizens; the sense of a canon of works in performance first appeared in 18th-century England.

Rooted in the patronage of church and royal court, surviving early medieval music is chiefly religious, monophonic, and vocal. The earliest extant manuscripts date from the [[Carolingian Empire]] (800–887), when Western plainchant gradually unified into [[Gregorian chant]]. Staff notation developed in the 11th century. By the mid-12th century France was the major European musical center, where the Notre-Dame school first fully explored organized rhythms and polyphony. In the early 15th century the Franco-Flemish School brought choral music, particularly the mass and motet, to new standards.

The [[Baroque]] period (1580–1750) saw standardization of common-practice tonality and growth of instrumental ensembles. Italy was the birthplace of opera, the concerto, sonata form, the oratorio, and the cantata, and the fugue technique championed by [[Johann Sebastian Bach]] exemplified the period's complexity. In the Classical period (1750–1820), [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart]], Joseph Haydn, and [[Ludwig van Beethoven]] produced symphonies, string quartets, and concertos. Romantic music (1800–1910) emphasized programmatic works, virtuosity, and nationalism, converging in the operas of [[Richard Wagner]].

In the 20th century stylistic unification dissolved and popular music grew in prominence. Many composers adopted modernism, some abandoning tonality for serialism. After World War II audiences for the first time valued older music over contemporary works. Composers from the Americas, Africa, and Asia now hold crucial roles, and symphony orchestras and opera houses appear across the world.

Queen of Ptolemaic Egypt (r. 51–30 BC) and the last active Hellenistic pharaoh.

Formally Cleopatra VII Thea Philopator, she was a member of the Ptolemaic dynasty and a descendant of its founder, [[Ptolemy I Soter]], a Macedonian Greek general under [[Alexander the Great]]. Her first language was Koine Greek, and she is the only Ptolemaic ruler known to have learned the Egyptian language, among several others.

Born in Alexandria, she was the daughter of Ptolemy XII Auletes, who named her his heir before his death in 51 BC. She began her reign alongside her brother Ptolemy XIII, but a falling-out led to civil war. After losing the 48 BC Battle of Pharsalus, the Roman statesman Pompey fled to Egypt and was ambushed and killed on Ptolemy XIII's orders. [[Julius Caesar]] then occupied Alexandria and was besieged with Cleopatra at the palace; after reinforcements lifted the siege, Ptolemy XIII drowned in the Nile. Caesar declared Cleopatra and her brother Ptolemy XIV joint rulers, and their private affair produced a son, Caesarion. After Caesar's assassination and Ptolemy XIV's sudden death, she named Caesarion co-ruler.

In the civil war of 43–42 BC she sided with the Second Triumvirate formed by Octavian, Mark Antony, and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. After meeting at Tarsos in 41 BC she and Antony had an affair that produced three children. Antony came to rely on her for funding and military aid in his invasions of the Parthian Empire and Armenia. The Donations of Alexandria declared their children rulers over various territories under Antony's authority, which Octavian portrayed as treason. He declared war on Cleopatra, defeated her and Antony's fleet at the 31 BC Battle of Actium, and invaded Egypt in 30 BC. Antony committed suicide; Cleopatra reportedly killed herself, probably by poisoning, to avoid being displayed in a Roman triumphal procession. Egypt became a Roman province, ending the Hellenistic period.

Roman historiography and Latin poetry produced a generally critical view of her that pervaded medieval and Renaissance literature. She has been depicted in Roman busts, coinage, and reliefs, in Renaissance and Baroque operas, paintings, and plays, and in Hollywood films, and has been a popular icon of Egyptomania since the Victorian era.

Long-term weather pattern of a region, typically averaged over 30 years.

More rigorously, climate is the mean and variability of meteorological variables over a span from months to millions of years. The variables most commonly measured are temperature, humidity, atmospheric pressure, wind, and precipitation. In a broader sense, climate is the state of the whole climate system: the atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, lithosphere, and biosphere and the interactions among them. The word derives from Ancient Greek *klima*, 'inclination'. The standard averaging period of 30 years was defined by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), whose technical commission designated 1901–30 as the reference period for standard climate normals in 1934. The 1961–90 normals serve as the baseline reference period. The popular phrase "Climate is what you expect, weather is what you get" summarizes the difference between climate and weather.

A location's climate is affected by its latitude, longitude, terrain, altitude, land use, and nearby bodies of water and their currents. Over historical time spans these determinants are nearly constant and change only over millions of years through processes such as plate tectonics. Others are more dynamic: thermohaline circulation of the ocean warms the northern Atlantic Ocean by 5 °C (9 °F) compared with other ocean basins, other ocean currents redistribute heat regionally, and vegetation affects heat absorption, water retention, and rainfall. Changes in atmospheric greenhouse gases, particularly carbon dioxide and methane, determine how much solar energy the planet retains.

Climates are classified by average and typical variables, most commonly temperature and precipitation. The most widely used scheme is the Köppen climate classification, first developed in 1899, which was designed to identify climates associated with certain biomes. The Thornthwaite system, in use since 1948, adds evapotranspiration, and the Bergeron and Spatial Synoptic systems focus on the origin of air masses. Originally, climes were defined in Ancient Greece by a location's latitude. A common shortcoming of all such schemes is that they draw distinct boundaries, while real climates change gradually.

Paleoclimatology studies past climates. Because few direct observations exist before the 19th century, it relies on proxy evidence: sediments, ice cores, pollen, and rocks, as well as tree rings and coral. Climate models are mathematical models of past, present, and future climates.

Long-term shift in Earth's temperatures and weather patterns, now chiefly the human-driven rise in global average temperature and its wider effects.

Present-day climate change includes both global warming, the ongoing increase in global average temperature, and its effects on the climate system. In a broader sense the term also covers earlier natural changes. The modern rise is driven by human activities, especially burning of [[Fossil fuel|fossil fuels]] (coal, oil, and natural gas) since the [[Industrial Revolution]]. Fossil fuel use, deforestation, and some agricultural and industrial practices release [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gases]], which absorb heat radiated by the Earth. The atmosphere now holds roughly 50% more carbon dioxide than at the end of the pre-industrial era, at levels not seen for millions of years. Between the 18th century and 1970 there was little net warming, because greenhouse warming was offset by cooling from sulfur dioxide emissions. The term *global warming* became popular after NASA scientist James Hansen used it in 1988 testimony in the U.S. Senate.

The year 2024 was the warmest on record, at +1.60 °C (2.88 °F) since regular tracking began in 1850. Heat waves and wildfires are becoming more common. Amplified warming in the [[Arctic]] has contributed to thawing [[Permafrost|permafrost]], retreat of glaciers, and sea ice decline. Higher temperatures are also causing more intense storms and droughts, and forcing many species to relocate or become extinct. Ocean heating, ocean acidification, and sea level rise will continue for centuries even if warming is limited. The World Health Organization calls climate change one of the biggest threats to global health in the 21st century. Poorer communities contribute a small share of emissions yet have the least ability to adapt.

The scientific literature shows broad agreement that human activities are the main driver of recent warming; debates continue over the precise value of climate sensitivity and the performance of climate models. Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, nations agreed to keep warming "well under 2 °C", but with current pledges warming would still reach about 2.8 °C (5.0 °F) by the end of the century. Proposed responses include ending fossil fuel subsidies, conserving energy, switching to wind, solar, hydro, and nuclear power, and removing carbon from the atmosphere through increased forest cover and soil-carbon farming.

Device that measures and displays time.

The clock is one of the oldest human inventions, meeting the need to measure intervals shorter than the day, the lunar month, and the year. The word derives from the medieval Latin *clocca*, 'bell'. A sundial shows time by the position of a shadow and was widely used in ancient times; sundials were used to check clocks until the 1830s. Duration timers include candle clocks, incense clocks, and the hourglass. Water clocks are possibly the oldest time-measuring instruments after sundials: the bowl-shaped outflow clock is known from Babylon and Egypt around the 16th century BC. The Greeks and Romans improved their accuracy, and the Chinese had developed advanced water clocks by AD 725. Su Song's water-driven clock tower, built in 1088, incorporated an escapement.

The invention of the verge escapement made possible the first mechanical clocks, around 1300 in Europe, which kept time with oscillating timekeepers such as balance wheels. Spring-driven clocks appeared in the 15th century. Accuracy improved after 1656 with the pendulum clock of Christiaan Huygens, and the importance of precise timekeeping for navigation stimulated further advances. The electric clock was patented in 1840. Electronic clocks appeared in the 20th century and became widespread with small battery-powered semiconductor devices. The quartz clock, invented in 1927 by Warren Marrison at Bell Telephone Laboratories, used the vibrations of a quartz crystal.

The timekeeping element of every modern clock is a harmonic oscillator, a resonator that vibrates at a particular frequency: a pendulum, balance wheel, tuning fork, quartz crystal, or the vibration of electrons in atoms emitting microwaves. The last is so precise that it defines the second; since 1967 the second has been defined by 9,192,631,770 cycles of cesium-133. Atomic clocks provide the standard for Coordinated Universal Time.

Analog clocks show time with a face and moving hands, while digital clocks display numerals, usually in 12-hour or 24-hour notation. Speaking clocks announce the time aloud, and tactile clocks serve the blind.

Items worn on the body, also called clothes, garments, dress, apparel, or attire.

Clothing is typically made from textiles but may also be made from animal skins, furs, other natural materials, and synthetic fibers. It is a feature of every known human society, and its form and use vary with climate, culture, available materials, technology, social norms, and individual preference. It serves protective, physiological, social, and cultural functions: comfort, thermal regulation, protection from environmental hazards, and specialized protection for occupations, sports, and other activities. It also expresses social status, gender, cultural identity, religious affiliation, modesty, and personal style, and is central to fashion.

Estimates of when humans began wearing clothes range from 40,000 to as many as 3 million years ago. A 2003 study suggested at least 100,000 years ago, based on the divergence of the body louse, which cannot survive outside clothing, from the head louse; this has been dated to between 40,000 and 170,000 years before present, although later genetic analyses cast doubt on lice as a dating method. In September 2021 scientists reported evidence of clothes being made 120,000 years ago from deposits in Morocco. Early garments were likely fur, leather, leaves, or grass draped, wrapped, or tied around the body; knowledge of them remains inferential because such materials deteriorate quickly. Bone and ivory sewing needles from about 30,000 BC were found near Kostenki, Russia, and a needle at least 50,000 years old made by Denisovans was identified at Denisova Cave in Siberia. Dyed flax fibers from 34,000 BC have been found in a cave in Georgia. The oldest known piece of woven clothing is the Tarkhan dress, a linen garment over 5000 years old.

Some cultures, including those in the Arctic Circle, have historically made garments solely from treated animal furs and skins. Others use textiles woven, knitted, or twined from fibers such as linen, wool, cotton, silk, hemp, and ramie. The textile industry was the first to be mechanized, with the powered loom, during the Industrial Revolution. Garments may be draped from uncut rectangles of cloth, as with the dhoti, sari, Scottish kilt, and Javanese sarong, or cut and sewn by hand or sewing machine to the wearer's measurements.

Clothing production has become one of the world's largest industries, employing millions of people and playing an important role in global trade, while facing challenges related to working conditions and sustainability.

Visible mass of liquid droplets, ice crystals, or other particles suspended in the atmosphere of a planetary body.

In meteorology a cloud is an aerosol composed primarily of water droplets and crystals. On Earth, clouds form when air is cooled to its dew point, or gains enough moisture, usually water vapor, to raise the dew point to the ambient temperature. Clouds occur in the homosphere, which includes the troposphere, stratosphere, and mesosphere. Nephology is the science of clouds, part of cloud physics within meteorology. The word derives from the Old English *clud* or *clod*, meaning a hill or mass of stone.

Tropospheric clouds have Latin names under the nomenclature proposed by Luke Howard in 1802, which became the basis of the modern international system of the World Meteorological Organization. It divides clouds into five physical forms (stratiform, cumuliform, stratocumuliform, cumulonimbiform, and cirriform) and classifies them by altitude to give ten basic genera. Mid-level types take the prefix *alto-* and high-level types *cirro-*. The ten genera include cirrus, cirrostratus, cirrocumulus, altocumulus, altostratus, cumulus, stratus, stratocumulus, nimbostratus, and cumulonimbus. Very low stratiform clouds reaching the ground are called fog and mist. In the stratosphere and mesosphere, clouds have common names and are seen infrequently, mostly in polar regions. Clouds on other planets and moons of the Solar System are often composed of other substances, such as methane, ammonia, and sulfuric acid, as well as water.

Around 340 BC [[Aristotle]] wrote *Meteorologica*, the first known systematic treatment of meteorological topics; the first truly scientific studies of clouds were made at the beginning of the 19th century by Howard in England and Jean-Baptiste Lamarck in France.

Clouds affect the Earth's climate. They can reflect incoming sunlight, cooling the surface, or trap longwave radiation from the surface, warming it; altitude, form, and thickness determine which effect dominates locally. Clouds are the main uncertainty in climate sensitivity.

Combustible black or brownish-black sedimentary rock formed as layers called coal seams.

Coal is mostly carbon with variable amounts of hydrogen, sulfur, oxygen, and nitrogen. It is a [[Fossil fuel|fossil fuel]], formed when plants decay into [[Peat|peat]], which is converted into coal by the heat and pressure of deep burial over millions of years, a process called coalification. Grade depends on the maximum temperature and pressure reached: lignite (brown coal) forms under relatively mild conditions, followed in turn by sub-bituminous coal, bituminous coal, and anthracite (hard coal). Temperature matters more than pressure or burial time; sub-bituminous coal can form at 35 to 80 °C (95 to 176 °F), while anthracite requires at least 180 to 245 °C (356 to 473 °F). The word derives from the Old English *col*.

About 90% of all coal beds were deposited in the [[Carboniferous]] and [[Permian]] periods, during the Late Paleozoic icehouse. Falling sea level exposed continental shelves, and wide river deltas formed, giving extensive wetlands ideal for coal formation. Oxygen levels above 30% promoted wildfires and charcoal that decomposers could scarcely digest, and lycophyte trees did not tie up carbon in heartwood for long periods. Coal is rare after the Permian–Triassic extinction event.

Coal is used primarily as a fuel, and some iron and steel-making and other industrial processes burn it. It was known and used for thousands of years, but use was limited until the [[Industrial Revolution]], and the invention of the steam engine increased consumption. In 2020 coal supplied about a quarter of the world's primary energy and over a third of its electricity. China, which mines almost half the world's coal, is the largest consumer and importer, followed by India with about a tenth; Indonesia and Australia export the most, followed by Russia.

Extraction and burning of coal damage the environment and human health, causing premature death and illness, and coal is the largest source of carbon dioxide contributing to climate change. Over 15 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide were emitted by burning coal in 2024, more than a quarter of total global greenhouse gas emissions. A record amount was burnt in 2024, but consumption is expected to peak before 2030. Supporters of coal point to the affordable energy access it has provided. Many countries have reduced or eliminated coal power, and the Glasgow Climate Pact agreed to phase down coal.

Dark, bitter, stimulating beverage brewed from roasted, ground coffee beans.

The beans are seeds of the fruits of the *Coffea* plant, a genus of the family Rubiaceae. After the seeds are separated from the cherries to produce green coffee, they are roasted, ground, and typically steeped in hot water before being filtered out. Its stimulating effect results from its caffeine content, although decaffeinated coffee is also available. Coffee is usually served hot, though iced coffee is common, and is prepared as espresso, French press, caffè latte, or canned coffee, often with sugar, milk, or cream. The word entered English in 1582 via Dutch *koffie*, from Ottoman Turkish *kahve* and Arabic *qahwah*, which most likely meant 'the dark one'.

Coffee has a history tied to food traditions around the Red Sea. The earliest reports of coffee drinking concern its use among Sufis of Yemen in the middle of the 15th century, and there is no confirmed evidence of the drink before the 15th century. Legends of its discovery, such as that of a goatherd named Kaldi, lack evidence; the Kaldi story does not appear before 1671. Abd al-Qadir al-Jaziri asserted in 1587 that coffee reached Cairo at the start of the 16th century. Until the end of the 17th century most of the world's coffee came from Yemen. Cultivation began in Java in the 17th century and in the Americas from the 18th century.

The two most commonly grown species are *C. arabica* and *C. robusta*. Coffee is cultivated in over 70 countries, mainly in the equatorial regions of the Americas, Southeast Asia, the Indian subcontinent, and Africa, and green coffee is traded as an agricultural commodity. The global coffee industry was worth US$495.50 billion in 2023, when Brazil was the leading grower, producing 31% of the world's total, followed by Vietnam.

Although sales reach billions of dollars annually, coffee farmers disproportionately live in poverty. Critics of the industry point to its environmental impact, including land clearing and water use.
